extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy; general readers of Hobbes' Leviathan
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Hobbes' laws of nature, the nature of rights, covenants, justice, and related social-legal rules from Leviathan (Gutenberg edition). Extracts the normative criteria Hobbes gives for when promises, covenants, rights, and obligations are valid or void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Right: every man has right to everything
rubrics_metrics.description: In the state of nature (a war of every one against every one), 'every man has a Right to every thing; even to one anothers body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes uses this to show why there can be no security or propriety absent covenant or common power; this right endures as long as the natural condition of war continues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Law of Nature: seek peace and defend oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: A general rule of reason: 'That every man, ought to endeavour Peace, as farre as he has hope of obtaining it; and when he cannot obtain it, that he may seek, and use, all helps, and advantages of Warre.' The first branch is 'To seek Peace, and follow it.' The second is 'By all means we can, to defend our selves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This law frames subsequent duties: effort toward peace is primary, but self-preservation permits resort to war when peace is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Law of Nature: lay down rights for peace (Golden Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man should be willing, when others are so, 'to lay down this right to all things; and be contented with so much liberty against other men, as he would allow other men against himselfe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reciprocal renunciation of unlimited natural right is necessary to move from war to peace; if others won't renounce, one need not either. Hobbes links this to the Gospel and classical precept ('Quod tibi feiri non vis, alteri ne feceris').

rubrics_metrics.name: What it is to lay down a right
rubrics_metrics.description: To lay down a man's Right is 'to Devest himselfe of the Liberty, of hindring another of the benefit of his own Right to the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laying down a right does not create a new right in another but removes impediments to the other's enjoyment; effect is diminution of obstacles rather than conferring an original right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of abandoning/transferring right and resulting obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Right is laid aside either by simply renouncing it (careth not to whom benefit redoundeth) or by transferring it to another (intending benefit to certain person(s)); once abandoned/transferred the actor is 'OBLIGED, or BOUND' not to hinder beneficiaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such voluntary acts create DUTY; undoing them is INJUSTICE because it contradicts what one voluntarily did. The signs must be voluntary and sufficient (words/actions). The bonds rest on fear of consequences rather than inherent strength of word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts: mutual transferring of right
rubrics_metrics.description: The mutual transferring of Right between parties is called CONTRACT; distinct from transfer/delivery of the thing itself (tradition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts may involve immediate delivery or deferred performance; the form shapes obligations like covenant, promise, keeping of promise, violation of faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenant: contract with deferred performance (pact)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one party delivers now and the other performs at a determinate later time, it is called PACT or COVENANT; trusting the other to perform is 'Keeping of Promise' and failure (if voluntary) is 'Violation Of Faith.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covenant presupposes deliberation and future performance; obligations depend on reliability and enforcement context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free-gift vs Contract
rubrics_metrics.description: When transferring of Right is not mutual but given in hope of friendship, service, reputation, pity, or reward in heaven, this is a GIFT (FREEGIFT, GRACE), not a contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different legal/moral consequences: gifts are voluntary, and obligations like GRATITUDE (later law) arise from antecedent grace rather than covenant-based justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of contract — express
rubrics_metrics.description: Express signs of contract are words spoken with understanding (present, past, or future), e.g., 'I Give', 'I Have Given', 'I Will Give' (promise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes distinguishes tense: present/past words can transfer future right; future-tense bare promises are insufficient for free-gifts unless supported by other signs or mutuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of contract — by inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs by inference arise from consequences of words, silence, actions, or forbearance; generally anything that sufficiently argues the will of the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inferred signs include acting in reliance on a promise, conduct indicating assent, or circumstances like prizes where the offeror intended transfer despite future-tense wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free gift passes by words of present or past, not mere future promise
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of the future constituting a bare promise are insufficient for a free-gift: 'To morrow I Will Give' indicates the right remains until transferred by other act. Words of the present or past can transfer future right by the virtue of the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But future-tense words may pass right when other signs indicate intent (e.g., offering a prize). Hobbes gives linguistic examples (Volos Hoc Tuum Esse Cras vs Cras Dabo) to show different meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: In contracts, promise can be equivalent to covenant
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a promise is made after the promisor has already received the benefit for which he promises, the promise should be understood as if he intended the right to pass; thus a promise can be equivalent to a covenant and be obligatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports ordinary commercial dealings: a promise in exchange can obligate even if expressed as future performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit: performance first entitles due
rubrics_metrics.description: One who performs first in a contract 'is said to MERIT that which he is to receive by the performance of the other; and he hath it as Due.' Similarly, winning a prize or catching thrown money merits it as due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes merit in contract (condign/congrui): contract merit creates a right to claim; merit from a free gift/prize depends on the giver's benignity but may create a due once transferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants of mutual trust without common power are void
rubrics_metrics.description: If a covenant is made where neither party performs immediately but trust one another, 'in the condition of meer Nature... upon any reasonable suspition, it is Voyd'; only a common Power with coercive force can render such covenants valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that words alone cannot bridle passions without fear of punishment; performance-first parties are at risk unless a sovereign power enforces obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of fear making covenant invalid must arise after covenant
rubrics_metrics.description: A fear that would make a covenant void must be something arising after the covenant was made (e.g., new fact or sign of will not to perform); preexisting reasons that should have hindered promising cannot be later invoked to avoid performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits excuses for breach: one cannot rely on foreseen obstacles to repudiate an earlier deliberate covenant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to the end contains right to the means
rubrics_metrics.description: Transferring any Right includes transferring the Means of enjoying it, 'as farre as lyeth in his power' (e.g., selling land transfers herbage; selling sovereignty transfers right to levy money to maintain soldiers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sellers cannot later frustrate the buyer by withholding essential means (cannot turn away stream that drives sold mill).

rubrics_metrics.name: No covenant with beasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Covent with brute beasts is impossible because they do not understand speech or accept translations of Right; without mutual acceptance there is no covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates necessity of mutual intentionality for contractual obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No covenant with God without special revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot make covenant with God except by mediation of those to whom God speaks (revelation) or his lieutenants, because otherwise we cannot know whether our covenants are accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vows contrary to natural law are in vain; if commanded by natural law, the law, not the vow, binds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants concern only possible and future acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Covenant matter must be something to come and judged possible for the promisor to perform; promising the impossible is no covenant. If something later proves impossible which was thought possible, the covenant binds to the value or at least to genuine effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If obligation becomes impossible after contracting, parties are bound to the extent of value or to honest endeavor rather than absolute performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants discharged by performance or forgiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are freed of their covenants two ways: by Performing (natural end of obligation) or by being Forgiven (restitution of liberty, retransferring the right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance and forgiveness are explicit ends of obligation; forgiveness restores liberty as if the covenant never existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants entered under fear are valid
rubrics_metrics.description: Covenants made by fear in the condition of nature are obligatory (e.g., paying ransom or service for life), because one party receives the benefit of life and the other receives payment/service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even disadvantageous peace made from fear binds unless a new just cause of fear subsequently arises to renew war; prisoners of war and weaker princes bound by ransoms/peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Former covenant to one makes later covenant to another void
rubrics_metrics.description: A former covenant that has passed away one's Right makes a later promise to another void; if one has transferred the Right already, one has no right to pass it again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal priority of transfers matters: cannot bind what you no longer possess to transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenant not to defend oneself from force is void
rubrics_metrics.description: A covenant not to defend oneself from force is always void because no man can lay down his right to save himself from death, wounds, and imprisonment; such promises do not transfer the relevant right and are not obliging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: promises to refrain from resistance to being killed are unenforceable; authorities still escort criminals to execution despite prior consent because self-preservation overrides covenant in that respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: No man obliged to accuse himself
rubrics_metrics.description: A covenant to accuse oneself without assurance of pardon is invalid; in the condition of nature there is no place for accusation and in civil state accusation is followed by punishment (force) so one is not obliged to submit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony given under coercion or torture is not to be credited; confessions under torture relieve the sufferer, not inform the torturers reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath: form of speech added to promise; limits
rubrics_metrics.description: An OATH is a form added to a promise by which the promisor signifies that unless he performs he renounces God's mercy or calls for vengeance on himself; an oath taken in a rite other than the swearer's religion is vain. Swearing by what the swearer does not consider God is not an oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oath strengthens promise by invoking fear of divine revenge in the swearer, but Hobbes argues the oath 'addes nothing to the Obligation' if covenant is lawful; if unlawful it binds not even with oath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Law of Nature / Justice: perform covenants
rubrics_metrics.description: From the law commanding transfer of rights to avoid hindering peace follows 'That Men Performe Their Covenants Made' — without which covenants are vain and the right of all men to all things would remain; this is the origin of JUSTICE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes defines INJUSTICE as 'The Not Performance Of Covenant.' Justice is keeping valid covenants; where no covenant exists (state of nature) there is no injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice and propriety begin with commonwealth/coercive power
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice (and property) require antecedent covenant and the erection of a commonwealth with coercive power to compel performance; without such power there is no propriety and hence no injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes connects the moral-legal notion of 'giving every man his own' to institutional enforcement — justice presupposes a sovereign to enforce covenants and secure property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice is not contrary to reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping covenant (justice) is a Rule of Reason forbidding actions destructive to life; Hobbes rejects the claim that breaking covenants can be reasonable when it benefits self, arguing that breach undermines social ties and ultimately harms the breaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes rebuts sophistic arguments that successful wickedness equals virtue by showing breach of covenant is irrational for long-term preservation and societal membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covenants not discharged by vice of the person to whom made
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot reasonably claim that their covenant is discharged because the other party is vicious or unreliable; such faults ought to have been considered prior to making the covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that if the vice would have prevented making the covenant, it should have prevented making it in the first place; therefore character defects do not retroactively void promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice of men (manners) vs justice of actions
rubrics_metrics.description: When attributed to men, Just/Unjust refer to conformity of manners to reason; when attributed to actions, they refer to conformity of particular acts to reason. A just man strives to have just actions; unjust actions may not negate an otherwise just man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes moral character from specific culpable acts; sudden passions or mistakes may not change a person's general title 'just' or 'righteous'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing done to a man by his own consent is injury
rubrics_metrics.description: What is done conformable to a man's own will signified to the doer is no injury to him; if he had not passed away his original right, or has signified assent, then no breach of covenant or injury exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent (express or inferred) releases the doer from claims of injury; signifies release of antecedent covenant as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutative vs distributive justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice of actions is divided into Commutative (justice of contractors: equality/proportion in exchange and performance of covenants) and Distributive (improperly called distributive justice, more properly Equity: defining what is just when trusted as arbitrator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commutative justice concerns fair value in contracts (measured by appetite/contentment of contractors); distributive concerns allocation by an arbitrator, akin to equity — merit beyond contractual justice belongs to grace, not justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth Law of Nature: Gratitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Gratitude depends on antecedent grace (free-gift): 'That a man which receiveth Benefit from another of meer Grace, Endeavour that he which giveth it, have no reasonable cause to repent him of his good will.' The breach of this law is called Ingratitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gratitude supports benevolence and trust; without it mutual help and reconciliation cannot begin, which thwarts the first law's pursuit of peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth Law of Nature: Mutual accommodation / Compleasance
rubrics_metrics.description: Compleasance: 'That every man strive to accommodate himselfe to the rest.' People must temper asperities, adapt to others' differences, and avoid being so troublesome as to be cast out of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes uses an analogy of stones in a building: individuals whose manners take more room than they fill or cannot be corrected are rejected; complaisance is a practical social rule for coexistence.
